title: Chapter 187 – Tian Mo's Arm
html:
[The Gate Stair, Fifth Landing – Tian Mo]

For three weeks after the tide, Tian Mo wakes every morning with a hand he does not have.

It is always the left. He lies in the narrow cot in the guard-room on the fifth landing, in the gray hour before the lamps are lit, and feels the fingers curl. He feels the thumb press against the forefinger. He feels, in the palm, the old familiar callus where the staff has rubbed for twenty-three years. It is as real as the blanket on his chest. Then he turns his head, and sees the empty sleeve pinned to the wall beside him, and the hand is gone.

He has been told this is normal. Bell told him, in her flat plain way, with her fingers on his stump. The mind keeps the map after the body loses the territory. It fades. He nodded. He did not say that it has not faded, that if anything it has grown clearer, that some mornings he reaches out in his sleep and closes his phantom fist round the rail of the stair and wakes with his heart pounding because it was not there.

He sits up. He swings his legs over the side. He puts his bare right foot on the stone, and his bare left foot beside it, and breathes.

The stair is quiet. It has been quiet for three weeks. No ticking, no scraping, no slow dragging of heavy bodies in the dark. The roots in the walls have drawn back to a thin pale web, barely visible in the lamplight, and the blue lamps burn steady in their niches. At the foot of the landing, where a squat stone figure stands in its niche, a faint hum rises. The creature has not spoken since the night he was bitten. It has not moved either. But it has the look, he thinks, of something waiting for an instruction.

I am waiting too, he tells it silently.

He stands. He pulls on his tunic with one hand, which takes four minutes. He buckles his belt with one hand, which takes two. He takes the plain staff from its place by the door, grips it in his right fist, and walks out to the edge of the landing.

At the edge he plants his feet.

The staff wobbles.

He has tried a hundred times. It is simply not possible, with one hand, to hold a six-foot staff at the proper angle and keep it from drifting. It sways. It leans. It wants a second grip to pin it, and the second grip is gone. He sets his jaw. He plants harder, adjusts his stance, and drives the base of the staff into the stone.

It slips.

It skates a hand's breadth across the slick floor and nearly takes his foot. He catches himself on the rail, swearing under his breath, a word he has not used since boyhood, and stands there with his heart hammering and his one hand clamped white on the iron.

"Anyone can stand," he says, to the dark.

Nobody answers. Behind him, from the guard-room, a quiet voice says: "Not on one hand, Warden."

* * *

It is Dai, of course. She is standing in the doorway with a bowl of porridge and an expression he knows too well.

"Eat," she says.

"I'm not hungry."

"You're a liar." She holds it out. "Qinghe sent it herself. She said if I did not see you eat every bite, I was to bring you to the kitchen by the ear."

He takes it. It is warm, and gold, and faintly fragrant, and the smell alone makes his stomach turn over. He eats. It tastes of a spring morning and a long walk in the rain. When he is done, the shaking in his hand has stopped, and the dull ache in his stump has dwindled to a murmur.

"Better?" says Dai.

"Yes."

"Good." She sits on the edge of the cot without invitation and folds her arms. She has a new scar under her left eye, a pale curved line that gives her face a quizzical, amused look. "I have a thing to tell you."

"Tell me."

"You are being an idiot."

He looks at her.

"I mean it, Warden. With respect." She does not drop her eyes. "I have been watching you for three weeks. You get up before dawn. You go to the edge. You try to stand with a staff you cannot hold, and you fail, and you go back to bed and sulk. You've done it every morning. You think I haven't seen."

"I don't sulk."

"You sulk like a bull." She leans forward. "You are the best man I ever served under. You held the stair against a Rider. You lost your arm and you did not leave your post. You are, by any measure, a hero. And you are standing there every morning trying to prove to yourself that you are still the same man." She shakes her head. "You're not. You're a different man. And I think he's better."

"Dai—"

"Let somebody help you," she says. "That's all I'm saying. Let somebody help."

He sits for a long time with the empty bowl in his lap. The stair hums quietly beneath his feet.

"I don't know how," he says at last.

"That," says Dai, "is exactly what I thought."

* * *

Lin Kuang is waiting for him on the landing the next morning, with two wooden swords and a scowl.

"You can't fight with one hand," the boy says.

"No."

"But you can't just stand there either."

"No."

"So I'll fight you." Kuang tosses him a sword. Tian Mo catches it one-handed, which is a mercy; he did not expect the throw. "You hold the sword. I try to get past you. If I get past, I win. If you stop me, you win."

"That is the stair."

"Exactly."

They go at it for an hour. It is, Tian Mo thinks, the most useful hour he has spent in three weeks. He cannot swing the sword with any force. He cannot guard high and low at once. But he can stand, and shift his weight, and use his body as the wall it has always been, and Kuang's sword hits it and glances off, again and again. The boy is quick. He is thirteen and he feints and ducks and hurls himself at the gap on Tian Mo's left, where the arm should be, and the first three times he gets through.

The fourth time, Tian Mo steps into the gap, and takes him on the shoulder, and Kuang goes down on his back.

"Ow," says the boy, with great dignity.

"You overreached."

"I know." He lies there, grinning, looking up at the vault. "You moved your foot. You let me think the gap was bigger than it was."

"I did."

"That's cheating."

"That's the stair." Tian Mo offers him a hand, and pulls him up. "Everyone who comes to the stair thinks it is a door. It is a wall that has been told to look like a door."

Kuang rubs his shoulder, thoughtful. Then he says, in a very small voice, "Uncle Jian said I should learn from you."

"Did he?"

"He said you'd teach me how to stay when I wanted to run." The boy looks at the floor. "I think I'm going to want to run. When he's gone."

Tian Mo's chest tightens.

"You will," he says. "Everyone does. That's when you stay." He lays his one hand on the boy's head, briefly, and takes it away. "Get your sword."

* * *

Cheng Hui finds the record on the nineteenth day, in the lowest vault of the archive, and brings it to him in a cloth.

She is a thin serious girl in spectacles, nineteen going on sixty, who walks everywhere with a book under her arm. She lays the bundle on the table in the guard-room and unwraps it with great care. Inside is a sheet of yellowed vellum, crisp as a dead leaf, covered in faded characters in a script he does not know.

"It's the Founders' hand," she says. "I had it translated by Pei An's old colleague. It was in a box labeled Warden, miscellaneous. No one had opened it in two hundred years." Her eyes behind the lenses are bright. "It is a procedure."

"For what?"

"For this."

She lays her finger on a drawing at the bottom. It shows a man's torso, in the crude vigorous line of the Founders' illustrators, with a hanging left sleeve. From the shoulder, where the arm should be, a branching pattern spreads like the roots of a tree. A second figure stands beside him, squat and angular, with one hand extended.

"The Warden's Arm," says Cheng Hui. "Or so I read it. The oldest Gate-Keepers took injuries on the stair, as you did. When the flesh could not be mended, they asked the stair itself to lend them a limb. A root, a stone, a bone. It was made on the landing, in the dark, with the help of whatever guarded the stair." She swallows. "The guardian gave a hand. The roots gave the sinew. The Warden gave himself."

Tian Mo stares at the drawing.

"There is a cost," says Cheng Hui. "The record says so plainly. It lists three."

"Name them."

"The first is that the arm is not flesh. You will not feel heat or cold in it. You will feel pressure, and weight, and the stone beneath your hand, but not warmth." She hesitates. "The second is that it belongs to the stair. If you go beyond the reach of the roots, a mile, perhaps two, it will weaken. It will become dead weight."

"And the third?"

She does not answer at once. She takes off her spectacles, and polishes them on her sleeve, and puts them back.

"The third is that you can never leave," she says. "Not for long. Not for a season. The record calls it the Warden's vow. The arm will hold as long as you stand. When you cease to stand, it will cease. And it does not wait for you to die."

Silence.

He sits looking at the vellum. He thinks of the empty sleeve. He thinks of the long mornings, and the slipping staff, and the way his hand has closed on air for twenty-one days.

"When you say cease," he says slowly.

"The record uses the word unmake." Cheng Hui's voice is very quiet. "I'm sorry. I thought you should know."

He nods. He looks at the drawing a long moment. Then he pushes back his chair, and rises, and does something he has not done since the Night of Counting.

He laughs.

It is a short, rough, startled sound. It echoes in the guard-room.

"What is it?" says Cheng Hui.

"Nothing." He wipes his eye with the heel of his hand. "It's only that I have spent twenty-three years being told I was nothing but a man who stood. And now the Founders tell me I can be nothing but a man who stands, for ever, and be thanked for it."

"You can say no."

"I know."

"Nobody would blame you."

"No." He stands a moment longer, with his hand on the table. "But I think I would blame myself."

* * *

Jian comes to look at the procedure on the twenty-first day, and he sits for a long time with the vellum in his lap, saying nothing.

He is thinner. They are all aware of it, in the Garden, though no one says it. His hair is white now, not gray, and the skin of his face has drawn tight against the bone like parchment over a frame. But he holds himself straight, and his eyes are clear, and when he looks up from the page, Tian Mo sees something steady and sad and almost amused in them.

"It will work," he says.

"You're sure?"

"I'm sure." Jian lays the sheet on the table. "I looked, last night. I spent a day. I thought you would want the certainty." He smiles faintly. "It is a very elegant piece of craft. The roots will take the shape of the muscles. The stone will take the shape of the bones. The two will meet at the shoulder, in the socket, and learn each other. It will take perhaps six hours, and it will hurt more than anything you have felt."

"I have felt a Gnasher's jaws."

"This is worse." Jian pauses. "Bell will need the hours. She will need a quiet place. She will need Qinghe's broth every hour, and Yue's friend Mo Yan, who can hear the roots. And she will need you to be conscious for the whole of it. If you faint, the seam fails."

"Why?"

"Because the arm does not join to a body. It joins to a will." Jian leans back. "The Founders understood that. You are the stair. You always were. The arm is only the part of you that can reach."

Tian Mo is silent. He thinks of Hu's hand on his shoulder, twenty-three years ago, dry and hard as a root. You are the stair now. He had thought it a figure of speech.

"One more thing," says Jian. "The vow."

"I have read the vow."

"Then you know it is not light." The thin gray eyes hold his. "I would not ask you to take it for my sake. I would not ask you to take it for the Garden's, either. If you choose to do this, I want you to do it because it is what you want. Not what you owe."

Tian Mo thinks about this for a long time.

"Elder," he says. "May I tell you something?"

"Of course."

"I do not want to leave the stair." The words come out slowly, as though he is hearing them for the first time. "I thought I did. I thought I wanted to be free of it, to walk in the sun, to marry, to have a house with a garden. But I've lain in that cot for three weeks and what I dreamed of was the landing. The cold under my feet. The lamps. The sound the roots make." He swallows. "It is where I am whole. I did not know."

Jian does not speak.

"I think the vow is not a chain," says Tian Mo. "I think it is a name."

"Yes," says Jian, very softly. "I think so too."

* * *

They do it on the fifth landing on the twenty-third night, in the blue dark, with the whole stair watching.

Not literally. The guards have been sent away, all but Dai, who refused to go, and who stands at the head of the flight with her spear grounded and her face set. Bell kneels on the stone at his left, with a case of knives and a basin of steaming water. Qinghe sits behind, on a stool, with the black kettle on her knee, ladling broth into a cup at the first sign of a tremor. Cheng Hui holds the vellum. Mo Yan, the small silent girl with the charcoal behind her ear, sits cross-legged at his feet with her palm flat on the stone, humming.

And beside them all, in the lamplight, stands the stone creature.

It has descended from its niche. It moves with the slow gritting dignity of an old mill-wheel, and stops before him, and looks up. Its two chips of pale light meet his eyes. It does not speak. It holds out its remaining hand, a rough gray block of stone, palm up, and then, with a sound like a rock splitting, it brings the other, the broken stump, against its own chest.

A thin white crack opens.

A seam. A fault-line, running up from the wrist to the shoulder of the creature's remaining arm. It is giving itself. He understands that all at once. It is not lending. It is giving. There is a pause in the hum of the stair, a gap in the pulse, and he sees Mo Yan turn her head, and Yue's face in his mind, and Hu's.

"No," he says. "You don't have to—"

The creature looks at him.

Stand, it says.

It is the first word he has ever heard it speak. It comes not from the mouth but from the stone beneath him, a deep, grave, grinding syllable, and in it he hears every dusk he has ever stood on this landing.

He kneels.

He does it slowly, with his right hand on the floor. He presents his left shoulder, the empty, scarred, bandaged stump, to the old gray figure. And the creature lifts its hand, and lays it, with a surprising delicacy, against the place where the arm used to be.

It begins.

* * *

He will remember it, afterward, only in pieces.

He remembers the cold. A cold like a river, poured into the socket of his shoulder, spreading down through the bones. He remembers Bell's voice, low and steady: breathe. Breathe. Don't fight it. He remembers the roots coming. They came out of the walls without sound, slender and white, and wound themselves round the creature's hand and round his shoulder in a slow tightening web. He remembers the first pull. A grinding, tearing, wrenching sensation, as of a dislocated joint being forced back into place with a blunt mallet, and a roar that he realizes only later was his own.

He remembers Qinghe's spoon. The hot gold broth, poured between his teeth, going down like light. And Dai's voice, shouting at the top of the stair: Hold, Warden! Hold! And Mo Yan, humming, a thin high pure note that went through the pain like a thread through a needle and stitched it to something else.

He remembers a long dark stretch where nothing happened at all.

And he remembers, near the end, a voice.

You stood, said Hu.

It was not a ghost. It was not a dream. It was the dry, level, unhurried voice of a man who had spent forty years on the same landing and had run out of things to say. It came from the stair, from the roots, from the stone, and it was warm.

I did not think you would stay, it said. Most don't.

I almost didn't.

Almost is the whole of the work. A pause. I was proud, boy. I am sorry I never said so.

I knew.

Did you? The old voice almost laughed. Then you were wiser than I.

The cold in his shoulder broke. A hot bright pulse flooded outward, from the socket down through the roots and the stone into the long hard length of the new limb. He felt it fill. He felt it settle. He felt something move in the dark below his elbow, slow, powerful, patient.

He opened his eyes.

The landing was silent. The lamps burned steady. Bell was sitting back on her heels with her hands in her lap and her face gray with exhaustion. Qinghe had slid off her stool and lay curled on the floor, asleep, with the kettle in her arms. Dai had her face pressed into her sleeve. And before him, in the pale blue light, gleaming with a fine film of dew, stretched his left arm.

It was long. It was strong. It was the color of old ivory, veined with white, and where the skin should be there was a faint grain, like polished root. The hand at the end of it was broad and square and bore, he saw with a thick throat, the exact shape of the callus he had worn for twenty-three years.

He flexed the fingers.

They closed.

* * *

He tests it at dawn, on the edge of the landing, with a staff in each hand.

It holds. He sets his feet and plants the staff, and for the first time in three weeks, both hands lock round the shaft and it stands true. He drives it into the stone. It does not slip. He swings it, high, low, in the short hard circle of the old art, and the air whistles, and the left hand follows the right as if it had never been gone.

He cannot feel the warmth of it. It is true. The wood is neither cold nor hot to the left palm. It is only wood. But he feels the weight, the grain, the slight tremor of the shaft when it strikes the floor. He feels, through the stone, the whole stair, the seven hundred and one steps, humming up through the bones of his wrist.

"It's heavy," he says.

"That's the stone," says Bell wearily. She is sitting against the wall with a cup of tea. "It'll settle. In a month you won't notice."

* * *

Duan Ke finds him on the landing at mid-morning, and says nothing, and draws.

He does it without warning. The pale blade clears its scabbard with a soft rasp, and the boy is across the landing in two steps, the point leveled at Tian Mo's breast. It is a quick, hard, clean attack, the kind he would use on a man he meant to kill. Tian Mo has no time to think. He raises the new arm, and the blade strikes it, and the sound is like a bell.

The point stops.

It does not pierce. It does not even scratch. It skids off the pale root-grained surface with a ringing shriek and lodges, quivering, in the wall. Duan Ke stares. He looks at the sword, then at the arm, then at Tian Mo, and his sullen face does something it has not done in all the days since he came out of the Gate: it opens.

"Huh," he says.

"Was that a test?"

"I wanted to see." The boy wrenches the blade free. He turns it over, and examines the edge, and a faint pleased frown crosses his face. "It's good. It's very good. It didn't even notch." He sheathes it. "May I try again?"

"If you tell me why."

"Because I haven't hit anything in three weeks." The sullen look returns, but it is lighter now. "Everyone's too careful. They all think I'll break. You didn't."

Tian Mo almost smiles.

"Again, then," he says. "But slowly. Let's see how long we can make it last."

They fence for an hour, in the cold blue dawn, with the stone creature watching from its niche and the lamps flickering on the wall. The boy fights like a coiled spring. He is fast and angry and brilliant, and he has no patience for defense. Tian Mo gives him none. He stands, and absorbs, and lets the new arm do what it was made for: be the thing that does not move.

At the end Duan Ke is breathing hard, grinning, with sweat in his hair.

"Again tomorrow?" he says.

"If you like."

"I like." The boy sheathes the blade. He hesitates. "Warden. The arm. Does it hurt?"

"No."

"Does it feel like yours?"

Tian Mo considers it. He looks at the broad ivory hand, the square knuckles, the faint white veins like roots under bark.

"It feels like the stair's," he says. "And the stair is mine."

Duan Ke nods slowly. "That's all right, then," he says. And it is the closest thing to a kindness he has offered anyone in weeks.

* * *

Bell is still there at dusk, against the same wall, with another cup, when he comes back from the Dock.

"And the vow?" he asks. "What did you feel, when it closed?"

She is silent. Then she lays her hand over his, on the staff, and he feels it as pressure, only, and weight.

"It's there," she says. "I felt it close. There's a thread in the arm now, running down the stair to the Dock. I can't see it. But I can feel it pull." She squeezes. "You're tied, Tian Mo. To this place. To this stone."

"I know."

"Does it frighten you?"

He considers.

Behind him, the Garden is waking. He hears the clatter of pails in the courtyard far above, and the first thin notes of the morning bell. He hears Dai laughing at something. He hears, from the Dock, a faint low note, like a bell struck softly under water. And under all of it, deep in the new arm, he hears the stair itself, humming its one long patient syllable.

Stand.

"No," he says. "It doesn't frighten me."

He plants the staff, both hands on it, and looks down the long blue spiral of the steps, the lamps, the roots, the dark. And for the first time since the night of the Rider, the Warden of the Stair feels the whole of it come up through the soles of his feet and settle in him like a home.

"I am the stair," he says.

And the stair, quietly, agrees.
